title: Ἡ τοῦ πατρὸς πεῖρα
about: Odysseus sends his men to the house to kill a pig for the meal and goes alone into his father’s plot, meaning to try the old man before he says who he is. He finds Laertes digging round a plant, filthy and badly clothed, in patched leg-guards, gloves and a goatskin cap, and weeps at the sight. He decides to start with taunting words, praises the care of the orchard, finds fault with the old man’s own neglected state, and asks whose servant he is. Then, in a story that is false from start to finish, he says that he once entertained a man of Ithaca, who called Laertes his father, and gave him rich gifts. Laertes answers in tears that the gifts were wasted, for that guest is surely dead, unmourned and unburied far from home, and he asks the stranger who he is. Odysseus gives an invented name and country and says that Odysseus left five years ago. A dark cloud of grief covers Laertes, who pours dust over his head; Odysseus can hold back no longer, embraces him, and tells him that he is the man he mourns, home in the twentieth year and the killer of the suitors.

sentences.t:
ὑμεῖς μὲν νῦν ἔλθετ’ ἐϋκτίμενον δόμον εἴσω,
δεῖπνον δ’ αἶψα συῶν ἱερεύσατε ὅς τις ἄριστος·
sentences.l:
“You, then, now go into the well-built house,
and at once for the meal slaughter whichever of the swine is best;
sentences.i: “You go on now into the well-built house, and at once kill whichever of the pigs is best for the meal;
sentences.n: ὑμεῖς μὲν νῦν opens a speech with no introduction in this part: the previous part ended with the line that names the listeners, the servants and Odysseus’ son, so the opening quotation mark falls here. μέν is answered by αὐτὰρ ἐγώ in the next unit: ‘you … but I’. ἔλθετ’ is the aorist imperative of ἔρχομαι ‘go’, and δόμον εἴσω is ‘into the house’, εἴσω standing after its noun. ἐϋκτίμενον ‘well-built’ is the adjective used of houses and towns. ἱερεύσατε, from ἱερεύω, is the verb for slaughtering an animal for sacrifice and the meal that follows; ὅς τις ἄριστος is ‘whichever is best’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ πατρὸς πειρήσομαι ἡμετέροιο,
αἴ κέ μ’ ἐπιγνώῃ καὶ φράσσεται ὀφθαλμοῖσιν,
ἦέ κεν ἀγνοιῇσι, πολὺν χρόνον ἀμφὶς ἐόντα.
sentences.i: but I will put my own father to the test, to see whether he recognises me when he sees me, or fails to know me after so long away.”
sentences.n: πατρὸς … ἡμετέροιο is ‘our father’, the plural ἡμέτερος standing for ‘my’, as in ἡμέτερόνδ’ (267) and ἡμετέροισι (325). πειρήσομαι is the future of πειράω ‘make trial of’, with the genitive. αἴ κε is ‘if’ (αἰ is the by-form of εἰ before κε); the first alternative is ἐπιγνώῃ ‘will recognise’ and φράσσεται ‘will notice’, the second ἀγνοιῇσι, a subjunctive of ἀγνοιέω ‘fail to recognise’ in an old form with the ending -σι. ἀμφὶς ἐόντα agrees with an unspoken ‘me’: ‘being apart’, that is away, for a long time (πολὺν χρόνον). Odysseus’ plan is the test that the narrator says he adopts in 240. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν δμώεσσιν ἀρήϊα τεύχε’ ἔδωκεν.
sentences.l: So having spoken, to the servants warlike armour he gave.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and gave his warlike armour to the servants.
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’ closes a speech with an aorist participle; the Greek does not say why Odysseus gives up his armour, and neither does the translation. δμώεσσιν is the dative plural of δμώς ‘servant’, in the old ending -εσσι. τεύχε’ is the elided τεύχεα ‘armour’, and ἀρήϊα ‘warlike’ agrees with it. ἔδωκεν ‘gave’ is the plain aorist of δίδωμι.

sentences.t:
οἱ μὲν ἔπειτα δόμονδε θοῶς κίον, αὐτὰρ Ὀδυσσεὺς
ἆσσον ἴεν πολυκάρπου ἀλωῆς πειρητίζων.
sentences.l:
They then to the house swiftly went, but Odysseus
went nearer to the richly fruited plot, making trial.
sentences.i: They hurried off to the house, while Odysseus went on toward the richly fruited plot to make his trial.
sentences.n: κίον is the unaugmented past tense of κίω ‘go’, and δόμονδε has the suffix -δε ‘to’: ‘to the house’. θοῶς is the adverb of θοός ‘swift’. ἆσσον is the comparative of ἄγχι ‘near’, here with the genitive ἀλωῆς: ‘nearer to the plot’, and ἴεν is the unaugmented imperfect of εἶμι ‘go’. ἀλωή is a planted plot, here the whole of Laertes’ ground with its trees and vines; the translation calls it ‘plot’, and keeps ‘orchard’ for ὄρχατος, the planted ground inside it. πολύκαρπος is built like πολύχρυσος ‘rich in gold’: ‘rich in fruit’. πειρητίζων, from πειρητίζω ‘make trial’, takes up πειρήσομαι in 216; its object, his father, is left unsaid.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ εὗρεν Δολίον, μέγαν ὄρχατον ἐσκαταβαίνων,
οὐδέ τινα δμώων οὐδ’ υἱῶν·
sentences.l:
He found not Dolius, going down into the great orchard,
nor any of the servants nor of the sons;
sentences.i: As he went down into the great orchard he found neither Dolius nor any of the servants or the sons;
sentences.n: ἐσκαταβαίνων is ἐς + καταβαίνων, ‘going down into’. ὄρχατος is an orchard, the planted ground inside the ἀλωή. Δολίον is the accusative of Dolius; the old man of 225 is he, and the ‘sons’ (υἱῶν, genitive plural) are, by the sense, his sons, who have gone off with him. οὐδ’ … οὐδέ … οὐδ’ gives three negatives in a row: neither Dolius, nor any servant, nor any of the sons. δμώων is the genitive plural of δμώς ‘servant’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄρα τοί γε
αἱμασιὰς λέξοντες ἀλωῆς ἔμμεναι ἕρκος
ᾤχοντ’, αὐτὰρ ὁ τοῖσι γέρων ὁδὸν ἡγεμόνευε.
sentences.l:
but, as it turned out, they
to gather wall-stones, to be a fence for the plot,
had gone off, and the old man led the way for them.
sentences.i: but they, as it turned out, had gone off to gather stones to make a fence for the plot, with the old man leading them on their way.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄρα marks something now discovered: ‘but, as it turned out’; τοί γε is ‘they’, a pronoun and not the article. αἱμασιάς are the stones, or the dry-stone wall made of them; λέξοντες, the future participle of λέγω ‘gather’, says what they went to do. ἔμμεναι (= εἶναι) ἕρκος is ‘to be a fence’. ᾤχοντ’ is ᾤχοντο, the imperfect of οἴχομαι ‘be gone’, with the sense ‘had gone’. In αὐτὰρ ὁ τοῖσι γέρων, ὁ is the pronoun ‘he’ and γέρων ‘the old man’ is Dolius, who goes before the others (ἡγεμόνευε ‘was leading’, with ὁδόν ‘the way’).

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ οἶον πατέρ’ εὗρεν ἐϋκτιμένῃ ἐν ἀλωῇ,
λιστρεύοντα φυτόν·
sentences.l:
But his father alone he found in the well-built plot,
digging round a plant;
sentences.i: He found his father alone in the well-tilled plot, digging around a plant;
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ οἶον πατέρ’ is ‘and his father alone’: τόν is the pronoun ‘him’ and οἶον ‘alone’. ἐϋκτιμένῃ is the word translated ‘well-built’ in ἐϋκτίμενον δόμον (214); it belongs to houses and towns, and is stretched here to a cultivated plot, for which the free English says ‘well-tilled’. λιστρεύοντα is from λιστρεύω ‘dig about’, related to λίστρον ‘shovel’, and φυτόν is ‘a plant’, anything that has been planted.

sentences.t:
ῥυπόωντα δὲ ἕστο χιτῶνα
ῥαπτὸν ἀεικέλιον, περὶ δὲ κνήμῃσι βοείας
κνημῖδας ῥαπτὰς δέδετο, γραπτῦς ἀλεείνων,
χειρῖδάς τ’ ἐπὶ χερσὶ βάτων ἕνεκ’·
sentences.l:
and he was clad in a filthy tunic,
stitched, unseemly, and about his shins, of oxhide,
greaves, stitched, he had bound, avoiding scratches,
and gloves on his hands, because of brambles;
sentences.i: He wore a filthy, patched, unseemly tunic, with stitched oxhide leg-guards bound round his shins to keep off scratches, and gloves on his hands because of the brambles;
sentences.n: ῥυπόωντα ‘filthy’ is an uncontracted participle (Attic ῥυπῶντα), accusative singular, agreeing with χιτῶνα, which has three describers: ῥυπόωντα, ῥαπτόν and ἀεικέλιον. ἕστο, from ἕννυμι ‘clothe’, is ‘was clothed in’, with χιτῶνα ‘tunic’ as what he wore. ῥαπτός, from ῥάπτω ‘stitch’, is said of the tunic and again, in the feminine plural ῥαπτάς, of the leg-guards; ἀεικέλιον is ‘unseemly’. περὶ δὲ κνήμῃσι … δέδετο is tmesis, the preverb περί standing apart from δέδετο ‘had bound on’; κνήμῃσι is the dative plural of κνήμη ‘shin’. κνημῖδες are ‘greaves’, which here are of oxhide (βοείας) and not a warrior’s bronze; they are the word behind ἐυκνήμιδες ‘well-greaved’. γραπτῦς, a rare noun, is taken to mean ‘scratches’, from γράφω ‘scratch’; ἀλεείνων is ‘avoiding’. χειρῖδες are ‘gloves’, and βάτων ἕνεκ’ is ‘because of brambles’, ἕνεκα following its noun (βάτων is the genitive plural of βάτος).

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὕπερθεν
αἰγείην κυνέην κεφαλῇ ἔχε, πένθος ἀέξων.
sentences.l:
and above
a goatskin helmet on his head he wore, increasing his grief.
sentences.i: and on top of it all he wore a goatskin cap on his head, adding to his grief.
sentences.n: αὐτάρ is ‘and’, and ὕπερθεν ‘above, on top’. αἰγείην, from αἴξ ‘goat’, is ‘of goatskin’. κυνέη is the word for a soldier’s helmet, and the literal line keeps ‘helmet’; what he wears here is a cap of hide, which is what the free English says. ἔχε is the unaugmented imperfect ‘was wearing’. πένθος ἀέξων is ‘making his grief grow’: his squalid dress and the way he lives are themselves a sign of mourning, though the Greek says only that he was increasing his grief.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ὡς οὖν ἐνόησε πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεὺς
γήραϊ τειρόμενον, μέγα δὲ φρεσὶ πένθος ἔχοντα,
στὰς ἄρ’ ὑπὸ βλωθρὴν ὄγχνην κατὰ δάκρυον εἶβε.
sentences.l:
And when much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus noticed him
wasted with old age, and with great grief in his mind,
he stood then beneath a tall pear tree and let fall a tear.
sentences.i: When much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus saw him worn down with age and carrying a great grief in his mind, he stopped under a tall pear tree and let a tear fall.
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ ὡς οὖν ἐνόησε is ‘and when he noticed him’; ὡς without an accent is the conjunction ‘when’, and ἐνόησε is ‘noticed, perceived’. πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς is the standing name-formula ‘much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus’. γήραϊ τειρόμενον is ‘worn down by old age’, the dative of cause beside the passive participle of τείρω, and μέγα … πένθος ἔχοντα ‘having great grief’, both agreeing with τόν; φρεσί ‘in his mind’ is a dative plural. στάς is the aorist participle of ἵστημι ‘having stopped’. βλωθρήν ‘tall’ is the traditional gloss, its derivation not known; ὄγχνη is a pear tree. κατὰ δάκρυον εἶβε, ‘let a tear fall’, is the phrase that returns for Laertes in 280.

sentences.t:
μερμήριξε δ’ ἔπειτα κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμὸν
κύσσαι καὶ περιφῦναι ἑὸν πατέρ’, ἠδὲ ἕκαστα
εἰπεῖν, ὡς ἔλθοι καὶ ἵκοιτ’ ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν,
ἦ πρῶτ’ ἐξερέοιτο ἕκαστά τε πειρήσαιτο.
sentences.l:
And then he pondered, in mind and in heart,
whether he should kiss and cling round his own father, and each thing
tell, how he had come and reached his fatherland,
or should first question him and test him on each point.
sentences.i: And then he pondered in his mind and heart whether he should kiss and embrace his father and tell him everything, how he had come and reached his fatherland, or should first question him and test him out on every point.
sentences.n: μερμήριξε is the aorist of μερμηρίζω ‘ponder, be in two minds’; the same words, κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμόν ‘in mind and in heart’, introduce Menelaus’ hesitation over Telemachus in Book 4 (4.117), and the last line of this unit is repeated from that passage. The first alternative is expressed in infinitives (κύσσαι ‘to kiss’, περιφῦναι ‘to cling round’, that is to embrace, εἰπεῖν ‘to tell’); in the second the verb is an optative, ἐξερέοιτο ‘should question closely’. ἑὸν πατέρ’ is ‘his own father’: ἑός is the possessive ‘his own’. ἕκαστα is ‘each thing’. In ὡς ἔλθοι καὶ ἵκοιτ’ the two optatives stand in an indirect question after a past verb: ‘how he had come and reached’. πατρίδα γαῖαν is ‘fatherland’.

sentences.t:
ὧδε δέ οἱ φρονέοντι δοάσσατο κέρδιον εἶναι,
πρῶτον κερτομίοις ἐπέεσσιν πειρηθῆναι.
sentences.l:
And thus to him considering it seemed better to be,
first with taunting words to make trial of him.
sentences.i: And this, as he thought it over, seemed to him the better course: to test him first with taunting words.
sentences.n: The first line is a formula that closes a deliberation with a decision. δοάσσατο is an old aorist ‘it seemed’; φρονέοντι is the dative of the uncontracted participle φρονέων ‘thinking’, agreeing with οἱ ‘to him’; κέρδιον is the comparative of κέρδος ‘gain’, ‘more advantageous’ and so ‘better’. πειρηθῆναι is an aorist passive infinitive with an active sense, ‘to make trial’. κερτομίοις ἐπέεσσιν is ‘with taunting words’, the dative plural; the speech that follows is that test.

sentences.t: τὰ φρονέων ἰθὺς κίεν αὐτοῦ δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς.
sentences.l: These things thinking, straight toward him went heavenly Odysseus.
sentences.i: With this in mind, heavenly Odysseus went straight up to him.
sentences.n: τὰ φρονέων is ‘thinking these things’, τά a demonstrative pronoun. ἰθύς ‘straight’ takes the genitive of the person aimed at, as when Antinous goes ἰθὺς … Τηλεμάχοιο; αὐτοῦ is therefore the genitive of the pronoun, ‘him’, and not the adverb αὐτοῦ ‘there’. κίεν is the unaugmented imperfect of κίω ‘go’, which was seen in κίον at 220.

sentences.t: ἦ τοι ὁ μὲν κατέχων κεφαλὴν φυτὸν ἀμφελάχαινε·
sentences.l: Truly he, for his part, holding his head down, was digging round the plant;
sentences.i: His father, for his part, kept his head down and went on digging round the plant;
sentences.n: ἦ τοι is ‘truly, now’, and ὁ μέν is ‘he, for his part’, a pronoun answered by τὸν δέ in the next line. κατέχων κεφαλήν is ‘holding his head down’. ἀμφελάχαινε is the imperfect of ἀμφιλαχαίνω ‘dig round’, the same work as λιστρεύοντα in 227; the imperfect shows that it was going on while Odysseus came up.

sentences.t: τὸν δὲ παριστάμενος προσεφώνεε φαίδιμος υἱός·
sentences.l: And to him, standing beside him, spoke the glorious son:
sentences.i: His glorious son stood beside him and spoke to him:
sentences.n: τόν is the pronoun ‘him’, object of προσεφώνεε, the uncontracted imperfect of προσφωνέω ‘speak to’. παριστάμενος is the middle participle of παρίστημι ‘stand beside’. φαίδιμος ‘glorious’ is the stock epithet, here of Odysseus as υἱός ‘son’: the narrator names him by his relation to the man he is about to test. The speech that follows begins a new paragraph in Murray’s text.

sentences.t:
ὦ γέρον, οὐκ ἀδαημονίη σ’ ἔχει ἀμφιπολεύειν
ὄρχατον, ἀλλ’ εὖ τοι κομιδὴ ἔχει, οὐδέ τι πάμπαν,
οὐ φυτόν, οὐ συκέη, οὐκ ἄμπελος, οὐ μὲν ἐλαίη,
οὐκ ὄγχνη, οὐ πρασιή τοι ἄνευ κομιδῆς κατὰ κῆπον.
sentences.l:
“Old man, no inexperience holds you in tending
the orchard, but well for you the care holds, and not at all anything,
not a plant, not a fig tree, not a vine, nor an olive,
not a pear tree, not a bed for you without care throughout the garden.
sentences.i: “Old man, you are not unskilled at looking after an orchard, for your care of it is good, and nothing at all — no plant, no fig tree, no vine, no olive, no pear tree, no bed in the whole garden — is left without care.
sentences.n: ὦ γέρον ‘Old man’ is a courteous address to an older man. ἀδαημονίη is a rare noun, ‘lack of skill, inexperience’, the negative of δαήμων ‘knowing’; οὐκ … σ’ ἔχει ἀμφιπολεύειν is ‘inexperience does not hold you as to tending’, ἀμφιπολεύειν ‘to tend’ being formed from ἀμφίπολος ‘attendant’. κομιδή is ‘care, tending’ (the noun of κομίζω, see 251), and εὖ … ἔχει ‘is in good order’. The list in 246–247 repeats a negative six times: οὐ φυτόν ‘no plant’, συκέη ‘fig tree’, ἄμπελος ‘vine’, ἐλαίη ‘olive’, ὄγχνη ‘pear tree’, πρασιή ‘bed’ (a garden bed), and κῆπος ‘garden’. The speech is the ‘taunting words’ of 240: praise of the orchard, then the insults of the next lines.

sentences.t: ἄλλο δέ τοι ἐρέω, σὺ δὲ μὴ χόλον ἔνθεο θυμῷ·
sentences.l: And another thing I will tell you, and do not put anger in your heart:
sentences.i: But there is something else I will tell you, and do not harbour anger in your heart:
sentences.n: ἄλλο … ἐρέω is ‘I will tell you another thing’, ἐρέω being the future. μὴ … ἔνθεο is a prohibition with the aorist imperative middle of ἐντίθημι, in the old ending -εο (Attic ἔνθου): ‘do not put’; χόλος is ‘anger’.

sentences.t:
αὐτόν σ’ οὐκ ἀγαθὴ κομιδὴ ἔχει, ἀλλ’ ἅμα γῆρας
λυγρὸν ἔχεις αὐχμεῖς τε κακῶς καὶ ἀεικέα ἕσσαι.
sentences.l:
yourself good care does not hold, but at the same time old age
grievous you have, and you are unkempt, badly, and clothed in unseemly things.
sentences.i: it is you yourself who are not well cared for, and besides, you bear a grievous old age, and you are unkempt and dressed in unseemly clothes.
sentences.n: αὐτόν σ’ is ‘you yourself’, the object of κομιδὴ ἔχει ‘care holds’, now turned from the orchard to the man. ἅμα is ‘at the same time, besides’, and γῆρας λυγρόν ‘grievous old age’. αὐχμεῖς is from αὐχμέω ‘be dry, unkempt’, and κακῶς ‘badly’. ἕσσαι is the second person of the perfect passive of ἕννυμι, ‘you are clothed’, with ἀεικέα ‘unseemly things’ as what you are clothed in.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὲν ἀεργίης γε ἄναξ ἕνεκ’ οὔ σε κομίζει,
οὐδέ τί τοι δούλειον ἐπιπρέπει εἰσοράασθαι
εἶδος καὶ μέγεθος·
sentences.i: It is certainly not because of any idleness that your lord fails to care for you, and nothing slavish is to be seen in your form or your size;
sentences.n: οὐ μὲν … γε is a strong ‘certainly not’; ἀεργίης ἕνεκ’ is ‘for the sake of idleness’ (ἀ- + ἔργον), ἕνεκα following its noun with γε ἄναξ between them, and the second negative in οὔ σε κομίζει makes the whole ‘it is not because of idleness that he does not care for you’. ἄναξ is ‘lord’, unnamed: Odysseus speaks as if Laertes had an owner. κομίζω is ‘care for’. δούλειον ‘slavish’ is the subject of ἐπιπρέπει ‘shows itself’, and εἰσοράασθαι, the uncontracted infinitive of εἰσοράομαι, adds ‘to be looked at’. εἶδος καὶ μέγεθος, ‘in form and size’, are accusatives of respect.

sentences.t: βασιλῆϊ γὰρ ἀνδρὶ ἔοικας.
sentences.l: for to a kingly man you are like.
sentences.i: for you look like a kingly man.
sentences.n: βασιλῆϊ is the epic dative of βασιλεύς ‘king’, here used with ἀνδρί ‘man’, ‘a man who is a king’. ἔοικας ‘you are like’ takes the dative. The line gives the reason for the denial before it.

sentences.t:
τοιούτῳ δὲ ἔοικας, ἐπεὶ λούσαιτο φάγοι τε,
εὑδέμεναι μαλακῶς·
sentences.l:
And to such a one you are like, when he has bathed and eaten,
to sleep softly;
sentences.i: You look like a man who, once he has bathed and eaten, should sleep softly;
sentences.n: τοιούτῳ … ἔοικας continues the comparison: ‘you are like such a man’, and the man is described by two aorist optatives, λούσαιτο ‘has washed himself’ and φάγοι ‘has eaten’, and by the infinitive εὑδέμεναι (= εὕδειν, with the ending -μεναι) ‘to sleep’: one who is to sleep softly. The sentence ends at the stop after μαλακῶς ‘softly’.

sentences.t: ἡ γὰρ δίκη ἐστὶ γερόντων.
sentences.l: for this is the way of old men.
sentences.i: for that is the way of old men.
sentences.n: ἡ γὰρ δίκη ἐστὶ γερόντων: ἡ is the article used close to ‘this’, and δίκη here is what is customary, ‘the way’ of a class of people. The translation is the same as in other places in the poem where δίκη ἐστί names the way of a group (of servants, of mortals, of the gods). γερόντων is the genitive plural of γέρων ‘old man’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε μοι τόδε εἰπὲ καὶ ἀτρεκέως κατάλεξον,
τεῦ δμὼς εἶς ἀνδρῶν;
sentences.l:
But come, tell me this, and recount it exactly,
whose servant are you among men?
sentences.i: But come now, tell me this, and set it out for me exactly: whose servant are you?
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε μοι τόδε εἰπὲ καὶ ἀτρεκέως κατάλεξον is the standing request ‘But come, tell me this, and recount it exactly’, here with a comma and not a stop. ἀτρεκέως is ‘exactly’, and κατάλεξον the aorist imperative of καταλέγω ‘recount’. τεῦ is the interrogative τίνος ‘whose’ (Ionic), δμώς ‘servant’ is the predicate, and ἀνδρῶν ‘of men’ gives ‘among men’, as in τίς πόθεν εἶς ἀνδρῶν; at 298. The question ends at the question mark in the middle of 257; εἶς is ‘you are’.

sentences.t: τεῦ δ’ ὄρχατον ἀμφιπολεύεις;
sentences.l: and whose orchard do you tend?
sentences.i: and whose orchard is it that you look after?
sentences.n: τεῦ again ‘whose’; ὄρχατον is the orchard of 244–245; ἀμφιπολεύεις ‘you tend’ repeats the verb ἀμφιπολεύειν of 244. The two questions ask who the ‘lord’ of 251 is.

sentences.t:
καὶ μοι τοῦτ’ ἀγόρευσον ἐτήτυμον, ὄφρ’ ἐῢ εἰδῶ,
εἰ ἐτεόν γ’ Ἰθάκην τήνδ’ ἱκόμεθ’, ὥς μοι ἔειπεν
οὗτος ἀνὴρ νῦν δὴ ξυμβλήμενος ἐνθάδ’ ἰόντι,
sentences.l:
And tell me this truly, so that I may know it well,
whether in truth we have come to this Ithaca, as to me said
this man, who just now met me as I came here,
sentences.i: And tell me this truly, so that I may know it well, whether we have really come to this Ithaca, as this man told me when he met me just now on my way here,
sentences.n: καί μοι τοῦτ’ ἀγόρευσον ἐτήτυμον, ὄφρ’ ἐῢ εἰδῶ is ‘And tell me this truly, so that I may know it well’: ἀγόρευσον is the aorist imperative of ἀγορεύω, ἐτήτυμον the adverb ‘truly’, and εἰδῶ the subjunctive of οἶδα after ὄφρα ‘so that’. The same line returns whole in 297, where Laertes echoes Odysseus, and so it has the same English. εἰ here is ‘whether’; ἐτεόν is ‘truly’, Ἰθάκην τήνδ’ ‘this Ithaca’, ἱκόμεθ’ the aorist ‘we have come’. ὥς μοι ἔειπεν is ‘as he told me’; οὗτος ἀνήρ ‘this man’ points to someone Odysseus claims to have met just now, and who is not named. ξυμβλήμενος is the middle aorist participle of συμβάλλω ‘meet’ (ξυν- for συν-), agreeing with the man, and ἰόντι is the dative participle ‘to me as I was coming’. The unit stops at a comma because the sentence is too long to carry on.

sentences.t:
οὔ τι μάλ’ ἀρτίφρων, ἐπεὶ οὐ τόλμησεν ἕκαστα
εἰπεῖν ἠδ’ ἐπακοῦσαι ἐμὸν ἔπος, ὡς ἐρέεινον
ἀμφὶ ξείνῳ ἐμῷ, ἤ που ζώει τε καὶ ἔστιν
ἦ ἤδη τέθνηκε καὶ εἰν Ἀΐδαο δόμοισιν.
sentences.l:
not at all very apt-minded, since he did not dare each thing
to tell and to hear my word, when I asked
about my guest-friend, whether perhaps he lives and is,
or is already dead and in the house of Hades.
sentences.i: a man none too sound of judgement, for he did not dare to tell me everything or to hear what I had to say when I asked about my guest-friend, whether he is still alive and in the world, or is already dead and in the house of Hades.
sentences.n: ἀρτίφρων is formed from ἄρτιος ‘fitting, sound’ and φρήν ‘mind’; with οὔ τι μάλα, ‘not at all very’, it is a mild way of saying that the man had little sense. ἐπεὶ οὐ τόλμησεν is ‘since he did not dare’, with the infinitives εἰπεῖν ‘to say’ and ἐπακοῦσαι ‘to hear’, and ἕκαστα ‘each thing’. ἐμὸν ἔπος is ‘my word’, ὡς ἐρέεινον ‘when I asked’ (ἐρέεινον is the imperfect of ἐρεείνω ‘ask’). ξεῖνος here is the guest-friend, the man bound to him by hospitality. ἤ … ἦ introduces the alternatives ‘whether … or’; ζώει τε καὶ ἔστιν is ‘lives and exists’. εἰν is ἐν, and Ἀΐδαο the genitive of Ἀΐδης.

sentences.t: ἐκ γάρ τοι ἐρέω, σὺ δὲ σύνθεο καί μευ ἄκουσον·
sentences.l: For I will speak out to you, and you, take it in, and hear me:
sentences.i: For I will tell it out to you plainly, and you must take it in and hear me:
sentences.n: ἐκ … ἐρέω is tmesis for ἐξερέω ‘I will tell out’, the preverb ἐκ standing apart from the verb. σύνθεο is the aorist imperative middle of συντίθημι ‘take in, understand’, and μευ is the genitive of ἐγώ after ἄκουσον ‘hear’. The line is shared with an earlier passage and has the same English. From here Odysseus tells a false story about a man he once entertained; the man is Odysseus himself.

sentences.t:
ἄνδρα ποτ’ ἐξείνισσα φίλῃ ἐνὶ πατρίδι γαίῃ
ἡμέτερόνδ’ ἐλθόντα, καὶ οὔ πω τις βροτὸς ἄλλος
ξείνων τηλεδαπῶν φιλίων ἐμὸν ἵκετο δῶμα·
sentences.i: I once entertained a man in my own dear land, who came to our house; and no other mortal among friendly strangers from far-off lands has ever yet come to my house;
sentences.n: ἐξείνισσα is the aorist of ξεινίζω ‘entertain as a guest’; the verb returns in 271. φίλῃ ἐνὶ πατρίδι γαίῃ is ‘in my dear fatherland’. ἡμέτερόνδ’ has the suffix -δε ‘to’: ‘to our house’, the plural ἡμέτερος being used by a single speaker of his own house, as at 216. οὔ πω is ‘not yet’; ἄλλος ‘other’ and βροτός ‘mortal’ go with τις; ξείνων τηλεδαπῶν φιλίων is the genitive plural ‘of strangers from far-off lands, friendly ones’, a partitive. ἵκετο is the aorist of ἱκνέομαι ‘come’. The Greek does not add ‘so dear as he’.

sentences.t:
εὔχετο δ’ ἐξ Ἰθάκης γένος ἔμμεναι, αὐτὰρ ἔφασκε
Λαέρτην Ἀρκεισιάδην πατέρ’ ἔμμεναι αὐτῷ.
sentences.l:
And his birth he declared to be from Ithaca, and he said
that Laertes, Arcesius’ son, was his father.
sentences.i: He declared that he was Ithacan by birth, and kept saying that Laertes, the son of Arcesius, was his father.
sentences.n: εὔχετο … γένος ἔμμεναι is ‘he declared his birth to be’, εὔχομαι with an infinitive meaning ‘declare oneself to be’; γένος is ‘birth, family’. ἔφασκε is the iterative imperfect of φημί: ‘he kept saying’. Ἀρκεισιάδην is a patronymic, ‘son of Arcesius’, in the accusative with Λαέρτην, and ἔμμεναι αὐτῷ is ‘was to him’, that is ‘was his’. The guest of the false story is Odysseus himself, who is made to name Laertes as his father: Laertes is told, in the third person, of his own son.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν ἐγὼ πρὸς δώματ’ ἄγων ἐῢ ἐξείνισσα,
ἐνδυκέως φιλέων, πολλῶν κατὰ οἶκον ἐόντων,
καί οἱ δῶρα πόρον ξεινήϊα, οἷα ἐῴκει.
sentences.l:
Him I, to my house leading, well entertained,
kindly welcoming, many things being in the house,
and gave him guest-gifts, such as were fitting.
sentences.i: I took him to my house and entertained him well, welcoming him kindly, since there was plenty in the house, and I gave him guest-gifts such as were fitting.
sentences.n: ἄγων ‘leading’ and φιλέων ‘welcoming’ (φιλέω as a host, the uncontracted form of φιλῶν) are participles; ἐνδυκέως is ‘kindly’; πολλῶν κατὰ οἶκον ἐόντων is a genitive absolute, ‘many things being in the house’, that is, with plenty to give. πόρον is the unaugmented aorist ‘gave’, and δῶρα … ξεινήϊα is ‘guest-gifts’, ξεινήϊος being the adjective ‘of a guest’ agreeing with δῶρα. οἷα ἐῴκει is ‘such as were fitting’, ἐῴκει being the pluperfect of ἔοικα with the sense of an imperfect. The first two lines are the same words as an earlier passage and have the same English.

sentences.t:
χρυσοῦ μέν οἱ δῶκ’ εὐεργέος ἑπτὰ τάλαντα,
δῶκα δέ οἱ κρητῆρα πανάργυρον ἀνθεμόεντα,
δώδεκα δ’ ἁπλοΐδας χλαίνας, τόσσους δὲ τάπητας,
τόσσα δὲ φάρεα καλά, τόσους δ’ ἐπὶ τοῖσι χιτῶνας,
sentences.l:
Of gold, well-made, I gave him seven talents,
and I gave him a mixing-bowl all of silver, flowery,
twelve single cloaks, and as many carpets,
as many fine cloaks, and as many tunics besides,
sentences.i: I gave him seven talents of well-made gold, a mixing-bowl all of silver and decorated with flowers, twelve single cloaks and as many carpets, as many fine cloaks, and as many tunics as well,
sentences.n: The gifts are given as a list, and the unit stops at a comma after the fourth line because the whole sentence is six lines long. χρυσοῦ … ἑπτὰ τάλαντα is ‘seven talents of gold’, the genitive of the material; τάλαντον is a weight, not a coin. δῶκ’ is δῶκα ‘I gave’, and εὐεργέος ‘well-made’. κρητήρ is the mixing-bowl in which wine was mixed with water; πανάργυρον is ‘all of silver’, and ἀνθεμόεντα, from ἄνθεμον ‘flower’, ‘flowery’, that is decorated with flowers. δώδεκα … τόσσους … τόσσα … τόσους is ‘twelve … as many … as many … as many’. ἁπλοΐδας is ‘single’, of one fold, and so the opposite of a double cloak; χλαῖνα and φᾶρος are both ‘cloak’ in this translation, but the two garments are different. τάπητες are coverings spread over seats and beds, ‘carpets’. ἐπὶ τοῖσι is ‘in addition to these’.

sentences.t:
χωρὶς δ’ αὖτε γυναῖκας, ἀμύμονα ἔργα ἰδυίας,
τέσσαρας εἰδαλίμας, ἃς ἤθελεν αὐτὸς ἑλέσθαι.
sentences.l:
and apart, again, women, knowing blameless works,
four comely ones, whom he himself wished to choose.”
sentences.i: and, apart from these, four comely women skilled in blameless crafts, whom he himself wanted to choose.”
sentences.n: χωρὶς δ’ αὖτε is ‘and apart, besides’. γυναῖκας … ἰδυίας is ‘women … knowing’, ἰδυῖα being the feminine participle of οἶδα, with ἔργα as its object: ‘skilled in works’. ἀμύμονα is the stock epithet ‘blameless’; the meaning of ἀμύμων is not known, and ‘blameless’ is the traditional rendering. εἰδαλίμας is a rare word formed from εἶδος ‘looks’: ‘comely’. ἃς ἤθελεν αὐτὸς ἑλέσθαι is ‘whom he himself wished to choose’, ἑλέσθαι being the aorist infinitive middle of αἱρέω. Odysseus’ speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα πατὴρ κατὰ δάκρυον εἴβων·
sentences.l: Him then answered his father, a tear letting fall:
sentences.i: Then his father, letting a tear fall, answered him:
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα is the reply-formula ‘Him then answered’ (ἠμείβετο is the imperfect of ἀμείβομαι ‘answer’). πατήρ is Laertes, now named only as ‘father’. κατὰ δάκρυον εἴβων, ‘letting a tear fall’, is the phrase used of Odysseus in 234 (there as εἶβε): father and son weep in the same words.

sentences.t:
ξεῖν’, ἦ τοι μὲν γαῖαν ἱκάνεις, ἣν ἐρεείνεις,
ὑβρισταὶ δ’ αὐτὴν καὶ ἀτάσθαλοι ἄνδρες ἔχουσιν·
sentences.l:
“Stranger, truly indeed you have come to the country which you ask about,
but violent and wanton men hold it;
sentences.i: “Stranger, you have indeed reached the country you ask about, but violent and wanton men hold it;
sentences.n: ξεῖν’ is the elided vocative ‘stranger’. ἦ τοι μέν is ‘truly indeed’. ἱκάνεις is the present of ἱκάνω ‘arrive at’, with the sense ‘you have come to’. ἣν ἐρεείνεις: ἣν is the relative ‘which’ (feminine, agreeing with γαῖαν), and ἐρεείνεις is the verb of 262, ‘you ask about’. ὑβρισταί ‘violent’ and ἀτάσθαλοι ‘wanton’ both describe ἄνδρες (ὑβριστής is an agent noun used as an adjective); the second has the same root as ἀτασθαλίαι ‘wanton follies’ in the proem.

sentences.t: δῶρα δ’ ἐτώσια ταῦτα χαρίζεο, μυρί’ ὀπάζων·
sentences.l: and these gifts in vain you were giving freely, countless ones bestowing;
sentences.i: and it was in vain that you gave these gifts so freely, bestowing countless ones;
sentences.n: δῶρα δ’ ἐτώσια ταῦτα is ‘and these gifts … to no purpose’, ἐτώσια being a neuter plural adjective. χαρίζεο is the imperfect middle of χαρίζομαι ‘give freely, oblige’, without the augment (Attic ἐχαρίζου). μυρία is ‘countless things’ and ὀπάζων ‘bestowing’. Laertes calls the gifts wasted because, as the next lines show, he believes the guest who received them cannot repay them.

sentences.t:
εἰ γάρ μιν ζωόν γ’ ἐκίχεις Ἰθάκης ἐνὶ δήμῳ,
τῷ κέν σ’ εὖ δώροισιν ἀμειψάμενος ἀπέπεμψε
καὶ ξενίῃ ἀγαθῇ·
sentences.i: for if you had found him alive in the land of Ithaca, he would have repaid you well with gifts and sent you off with good hospitality;
sentences.n: εἰ γάρ μιν ζωόν γ’ ἐκίχεις is ‘for if you had found him alive’, with ἐκίχεις from κιχάνω ‘come upon, find’ in the past tense, a condition that did not hold. τῷ is ‘then, in that case’, and κέν with the aorist ἀπέπεμψε ‘sent off’ makes the result: ‘he would have sent you off’. ἀμειψάμενος is the middle participle of ἀμείβω, ‘having made an exchange’, here ‘having repaid’ with the dative δώροισιν ‘with gifts’; it is the verb of ἠμείβετο ‘answered’ with a different sense. δήμῳ is ‘land’, the district of Ithaca. ξενίῃ ἀγαθῇ is ‘with good hospitality’.

sentences.t: ἡ γὰρ θέμις, ὅς τις ὑπάρξῃ.
sentences.l: for that is the custom, for whoever may begin.
sentences.i: for that is the custom whenever someone has made the first move.
sentences.n: ἡ is the article used close to ‘that’, as in 255, with ἐστί left out. θέμις is what custom and the gods’ rule require, ‘the custom’. ὅς τις ὑπάρξῃ is ‘whoever begins’, ὑπάρξῃ being the aorist subjunctive of ὑπάρχω ‘begin’, here ‘begin with a kindness’: the man who first gives is owed a gift in return.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε μοι τόδε εἰπὲ καὶ ἀτρεκέως κατάλεξον,
πόστον δὴ ἔτος ἐστίν, ὅτε ξείνισσας ἐκεῖνον
σὸν ξεῖνον δύστηνον, ἐμὸν παῖδ’, εἴ ποτ’ ἔην γε,
δύσμορον;
sentences.l:
But come, tell me this, and recount it exactly,
which year in number is it, when you entertained that man,
your guest-friend, wretched, my son, if ever he was,
ill-fated?
sentences.i: But come now, tell me this, and set it out for me exactly: how many years ago was it that you entertained that man, your guest-friend, a wretched man, my son, if he ever was, my ill-fated son?
sentences.n: The first line is the standing request of 256, here again with a comma, now in the mouth of Laertes: he echoes Odysseus almost word for word. πόστον … ἔτος ἐστίν, ὅτε … is ‘how many years ago is it that …’: πόστος is the ordinal ‘which in number’. ξείνισσας is the aorist ‘you entertained’ (see 266, 271). σὸν ξεῖνον ‘your guest-friend’ stands beside ἐκεῖνον, and δύστηνον ‘wretched’, ἐμὸν παῖδ’ ‘my son’, εἴ ποτ’ ἔην γε ‘if ever he was’ (ἔην = ἦν) and δύσμορον ‘ill-fated’ are added one by one: Laertes speaks as if the existence of his son were in doubt. The unit ends at the question mark inside 290.

sentences.t:
ὅν που τῆλε φίλων καὶ πατρίδος αἴης
ἠέ που ἐν πόντῳ φάγον ἰχθύες, ἢ ἐπὶ χέρσου
θηρσὶ καὶ οἰωνοῖσιν ἕλωρ γένετ’·
sentences.i: Far from his dear ones and his fatherland, I suppose, either the fish ate him in the sea, or on dry land he became the prey of beasts and birds;
sentences.n: ὅν, ‘whom’, is the object of the first alternative, φάγον ‘ate’ (the unaugmented aorist of ἐσθίω), and the construction then changes: in the second alternative the man is the subject, ἕλωρ γένετ’ ‘became prey’, so the relative has no clean continuation, which the English cannot show. που is ‘perhaps, I suppose’. τῆλε φίλων καὶ πατρίδος αἴης is ‘far from his dear ones and his fatherland’: τῆλε ‘far’ takes the genitive, φίλων ‘dear ones’, and αἴης is the genitive of αἶα ‘land’, a by-form of γαῖα. ἠέ … ἢ is ‘either … or’; πόντῳ is ‘the open sea’, χέρσου ‘dry land’, θηρσί ‘beasts’, οἰωνοῖσιν ‘birds’ (datives), and ἕλωρ ‘prey’.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ ἑ μήτηρ
κλαῦσε περιστείλασα πατήρ θ’, οἵ μιν τεκόμεσθα·
sentences.l:
and not him his mother
wept for, having laid him out, and his father, we who begot him;
sentences.i: neither his mother, after laying him out, nor his father — the two of us who begot him — wept for him;
sentences.n: οὐδέ ἑ negates the whole clause, including πατήρ θ’ ‘and the father’ added after the verb: neither parent wept for him. ἑ is ‘him’. κλαῦσε is the aorist of κλαίω ‘weep for’, with an accusative. περιστείλασα is the aorist participle of περιστέλλω ‘wrap round’: the dead man would have been laid out and wrapped for burial. In οἵ μιν τεκόμεσθα, ‘we who begot him’, the verb is the first person plural of the aorist middle of τίκτω: Laertes speaks of himself in the third person (πατήρ) and then in the first (‘we’), since he and the mother together are meant.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄλοχος πολύδωρος, ἐχέφρων Πηνελόπεια,
κώκυσ’ ἐν λεχέεσσιν ἑὸν πόσιν, ὡς ἐπεῴκει,
ὀφθαλμοὺς καθελοῦσα·
sentences.i: nor did his wife, rich in gifts, sound-minded Penelope, wail for her own husband on the bed, as was fitting, closing his eyes;
sentences.n: οὐδ’ is ‘nor’. πολύδωρος is ‘rich in gifts’ (πολύ- + δῶρον), a rare word; the Greek does not say whether she brought many gifts or many were given for her. ἐχέφρων Πηνελόπεια is the stock phrase ‘sound-minded Penelope’. κώκυσ’ is the aorist ἐκώκυσε ‘wailed’. λεχέεσσιν is the plural of λέχος ‘bed’ used for one bed, here the bed on which the dead is laid out. ἑὸν πόσιν is ‘her own husband’: ἑός is the possessive again, easily mistaken for a relative. ὡς ἐπεῴκει is ‘as was fitting’ (the pluperfect of ἐπέοικα with the sense of an imperfect). ὀφθαλμοὺς καθελοῦσα is literally ‘having taken down his eyes’, the aorist participle of καθαιρέω: closing the eyes of the dead.

sentences.t: τὸ γὰρ γέρας ἐστὶ θανόντων.
sentences.l: for that is the prize of the dead.
sentences.i: for that is the prize of honour that belongs to the dead.
sentences.n: τό ‘that’ looks back to the weeping and the closing of the eyes. γέρας is a prize or share of honour, here what is owed the dead; θανόντων is the genitive plural of the aorist participle of θνῄσκω ‘die’: ‘of those who have died’. The line gives the reason for the whole of the sentence before it.

sentences.t: καί μοι τοῦτ’ ἀγόρευσον ἐτήτυμον, ὄφρ’ ἐῢ εἰδῶ·
sentences.l: And tell me this truly, so that I may know it well:
sentences.i: And tell me this truly, so that I may know it well:
sentences.n: This is the line Odysseus used at 258; Laertes now asks what Odysseus asked, in almost the same words (compare 256 with 287). Because the unit is the same as in an earlier part, it has the same English.

sentences.t: τίς πόθεν εἶς ἀνδρῶν;
sentences.l: Who among men are you, and from where?
sentences.i: Who among men are you, and where from?
sentences.n: τίς πόθεν εἶς ἀνδρῶν; is the question put to a stranger: ‘Who among men are you, and from where?’ εἶς, with its accent, is the second person singular of εἰμί, ‘you are’, and ἀνδρῶν ‘of men’ gives ‘among men’. πόθεν ‘from where’ has the suffix -θεν of place from which. The question is taken in two units, each ending at its question mark.

sentences.t: πόθι τοι πόλις ἠδὲ τοκῆες;
sentences.l: Where is your city and your parents?
sentences.i: Where is your city, and where are your parents?
sentences.n: πόθι τοι πόλις ἠδὲ τοκῆες; is ‘Where is your city, and where are your parents?’ πόθι is ‘where’ with the suffix -θι of place, τοι the dative ‘your’ (of possession, ‘to you’), ἠδέ ‘and’, and τοκῆες ‘parents’. The question is the second half of 298 and its English is the published wording of this line.

sentences.t:
ποῦ δὲ νηῦς ἕστηκε θοή, ἥ σ’ ἤγαγε δεῦρο
ἀντιθέους θ’ ἑτάρους;
sentences.l:
And where does your swift ship stand, which brought you here
and your godlike companions?
sentences.i: And where is the swift ship that brought you here, you and your godlike companions?
sentences.n: ποῦ δὲ νηῦς ἕστηκε θοή is ‘and where does the swift ship stand’: ἕστηκε is the perfect of ἵστημι with a present sense, ‘stands’, and νηῦς θοή is the stock pair ‘swift ship’, translated even though a ship at rest is not moving. ἥ is the relative ‘which’; ἤγαγε is the aorist of ἄγω ‘brought’, δεῦρο ‘here’, and ἀντιθέους … ἑτάρους ‘godlike companions’, an object beside σ’ ‘you’; ἑτάρους is the form of the word ‘companions’ that is shorter than ἑταίρους. The unit ends at the question mark inside 300.

sentences.t:
ἦ ἔμπορος εἰλήλουθας
νηὸς ἐπ’ ἀλλοτρίης, οἱ δ’ ἐκβήσαντες ἔβησαν;
sentences.l:
Or as a passenger have you come
on another man’s ship, and they, having put you ashore, went away?”
sentences.i: Or have you come as a passenger on another man’s ship, and they put you ashore and went their way?”
sentences.n: ἦ here opens a second question, ‘or’. ἔμπορος is ‘a passenger’, someone who travels on a ship not his own, as the words that follow say (νηὸς ἐπ’ ἀλλοτρίης ‘on another’s ship’, ἀλλότριος being ‘belonging to another’). εἰλήλουθας is the perfect of ἔρχομαι, ‘you have come’. ἐκβήσαντες is the aorist participle of ἐκβαίνω used causally, ‘having put ashore’, and ἔβησαν the aorist of βαίνω in its plain sense ‘went off’. Laertes’ speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to him:
sentences.n: The reply-formula: ἀπαμειβόμενος ‘answering’ and προσέφη ‘said to’ (the aorist of πρόσφημι). πολύμητις ‘of many wiles’ is a stock epithet of Odysseus built on μῆτις ‘craft’. The formula is the same line as elsewhere in the poem and has the same English. What follows is a long invention.

sentences.t: τοιγὰρ ἐγώ τοι πάντα μάλ’ ἀτρεκέως καταλέξω.
sentences.l: “Well then, I to you everything very exactly will recount.
sentences.i: “Well then, I will tell you everything quite exactly.
sentences.n: τοιγάρ is ‘well then, therefore’: it takes up Laertes’ request. ἀτρεκέως ‘exactly’ is the word of the standing request, and καταλέξω ‘I will recount’ the future of the verb in the imperative κατάλεξον (256, 287). The promise to tell everything exactly opens a false account, as the reader knows from 216, 240 and 265.

sentences.t:
εἰμὶ μὲν ἐξ Ἀλύβαντος, ὅθι κλυτὰ δώματα ναίω,
υἱὸς Ἀφείδαντος Πολυπημονίδαο ἄνακτος·
sentences.l:
I am from Alybas, where I dwell in famous halls,
son of Apheidas, Polypemon’s son, the lord;
sentences.i: I come from Alybas, where I live in famous halls, the son of the lord Apheidas, who was the son of Polypemon;
sentences.n: Ἀλύβαντος is the genitive of Ἀλύβας, the place Odysseus names as his home; no such place is known, and it belongs, with the other names in these lines, to the story he invents. ὅθι is ‘where’; κλυτὰ δώματα ‘famous halls’ is a stock phrase, and ναίω ‘I dwell’. In υἱὸς Ἀφείδαντος Πολυπημονίδαο ἄνακτος Ἀφείδαντος is the genitive that depends on υἱός, and ἄνακτος ‘lord’ and Πολυπημονίδαο, a patronymic ‘son of Polypemon’ naming Apheidas’ father, both agree with it.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ἐμοί γ’ ὄνομ’ ἐστὶν Ἐπήριτος·
sentences.l: and as for me, my name is Eperitus;
sentences.i: My own name is Eperitus;
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐμοί γ’ is ‘and for me, for my part’, and ὄνομ’ ἐστίν ‘there is a name’, with the dative of possession: ‘my name is’. Ἐπήριτος is another invented name; its meaning is not known.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά με δαίμων
πλάγξ’ ἀπὸ Σικανίης δεῦρ’ ἐλθέμεν οὐκ ἐθέλοντα·
sentences.l:
but some power drove me astray
from Sicania to come here, not willing;
sentences.i: but some power drove me off course from Sicania, so that I came here against my will;
sentences.n: δαίμων is an unnamed divine power, ‘some power’. πλάγξ’ is πλάγξε, the unaugmented aorist of πλάζω, used with an object: ‘drove astray’; the passive of the same verb opens the poem (πλάγχθη, ‘was driven astray’, in 1.2), so Odysseus gives his false self the word that began his own story. Σικανίης is ‘Sicania’, a place not otherwise known in the poem. ἐλθέμεν is the infinitive (Attic ἐλθεῖν), a result clause ‘so that I came’, with οὐκ ἐθέλοντα ‘unwilling’ agreeing with με.

sentences.t: νηῦς δέ μοι ἥδ’ ἕστηκεν ἐπ’ ἀγροῦ νόσφι πόληος.
sentences.l: And this ship of mine lies at her moorings out in the country, away from the city.
sentences.i: My ship lies at her moorings out in the country, away from the city.
sentences.n: The line answers Laertes’ question about the ship in 299. ἥδ’ is ‘this’, ἕστηκεν the perfect ‘stands’, which for a ship means that she lies moored; ἀγροῦ is ‘country’ and νόσφι πόληος ‘away from the city’ (πόληος is the epic genitive of πόλις). The same line is spoken in Book 1 by Athena, disguised as Mentes, in another false account of a ship.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ὀδυσσῆϊ τόδε δὴ πέμπτον ἔτος ἐστίν,
ἐξ οὗ κεῖθεν ἔβη καὶ ἐμῆς ἀπελήλυθε πάτρης,
δύσμορος·
sentences.i: And for Odysseus it is now the fifth year since he went away from there and left my fatherland, ill-fated man;
sentences.n: Ὀδυσσῆϊ is the dative ‘for Odysseus’ (ending -ῆϊ); τόδε … πέμπτον ἔτος ἐστίν is ‘this is the fifth year’. ἐξ οὗ is ‘since’. ἔβη is ‘went’ and ἀπελήλυθε ‘has gone away’ (perfect), the second line of the unit being a line shared with an earlier passage. Five years is a lie: Odysseus has come in the twentieth year (322). δύσμορος ‘ill-fated’ is said of the guest.

sentences.t:
ἦ τέ οἱ ἐσθλοὶ ἔσαν ὄρνιθες ἰόντι,
δεξιοί, οἷς χαίρων μὲν ἐγὼν ἀπέπεμπον ἐκεῖνον,
χαῖρε δὲ κεῖνος ἰών·
sentences.i: The birds were truly good for him as he set out, birds on the right, and I sent him off rejoicing at them, and he too went rejoicing;
sentences.n: ἦ τέ is ‘truly’, and ἐσθλοί ‘good’ agrees with ὄρνιθες ‘birds’; ἔσαν is ἦσαν ‘were’, and ἰόντι the dative participle ‘to him as he went’. δεξιοί ‘on the right’ is the lucky side for a bird seen at the start of a journey. οἷς is the relative ‘at which’ (dative plural), χαίρων ‘rejoicing’, and ἐγών the epic ‘I’. ἀπέπεμπον is the imperfect ‘was sending off’; κεῖνος is ἐκεῖνος ‘that man’, and χαῖρε ‘rejoiced’.

sentences.t:
θυμὸς δ’ ἔτι νῶϊν ἐώλπει
μίξεσθαι ξενίῃ ἠδ’ ἀγλαὰ δῶρα διδώσειν.
sentences.l:
and the heart of us two still hoped
to meet in hospitality and to give splendid gifts.”
sentences.i: and we two still hoped in our hearts that we should meet as host and guest and give splendid gifts.”
sentences.n: θυμός δ’ ἔτι νῶϊν ἐώλπει is ‘and the heart still hoped for the two of us’: νῶϊν is the dual dative ‘to us two’, and ἐώλπει a past form of ἔολπα ‘hope’ with the sense of an imperfect. The infinitives μίξεσθαι ‘to be joined’ (future middle of μίγνυμι) and διδώσειν ‘to give’ (a future infinitive, Attic δώσειν) depend on it, as verbs of hoping take a future infinitive. ξενίῃ is ‘in hospitality’, the dative of the bond between host and guest. ἀγλαὰ δῶρα is ‘splendid gifts’. Odysseus’ speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, τὸν δ’ ἄχεος νεφέλη ἐκάλυψε μέλαινα·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and him a cloud of grief covered, dark;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and a dark cloud of grief covered the old man;
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο ‘So he spoke’ closes the speech. τόν is the pronoun ‘him’, that is Laertes, the object of ἐκάλυψε ‘covered’ (aorist of καλύπτω). ἄχεος is the genitive of ἄχος ‘grief’, and νεφέλη ‘cloud’; μέλαινα ‘dark’ stands last and agrees with νεφέλη. A cloud of grief is Homer’s picture of sudden, blinding sorrow.

sentences.t:
ἀμφοτέρῃσι δὲ χερσὶν ἑλὼν κόνιν αἰθαλόεσσαν
χεύατο κὰκ κεφαλῆς πολιῆς, ἁδινὰ στεναχίζων.
sentences.l:
and with both hands taking sooty dust
he poured it down from over his grey head, groaning heavily.
sentences.i: and taking sooty dust in both hands he poured it down over his grey head, groaning heavily.
sentences.n: ἀμφοτέρῃσι … χερσίν is ‘with both hands’, the dative plural in -ῃσι. ἑλών ‘taking’ is the aorist participle of αἱρέω. κόνις αἰθαλόεσσα is ‘sooty dust’, dust of ash; pouring it over the head is a gesture of mourning. χεύατο is the aorist middle of χέω ‘pour’, without an augment. κὰκ is κατά, the final consonant taking on the κ- of κεφαλῆς: ‘down from over his grey head’. πολιῆς is ‘grey’. ἁδινά is a neuter plural used as an adverb, ‘heavily, thickly’, with στεναχίζων ‘groaning’.

sentences.t:
τοῦ δ’ ὠρίνετο θυμός, ἀνὰ ῥῖνας δέ οἱ ἤδη
δριμὺ μένος προὔτυψε φίλον πατέρ’ εἰσορόωντι.
sentences.l:
And his heart was stirred, and up through his nostrils to him now
a sharp strength burst forth, as he looked on his dear father.
sentences.i: His heart was stirred, and a sharp surge of feeling shot up through his nostrils as he looked at his dear father.
sentences.n: τοῦ δ’ ὠρίνετο θυμός is ‘and his heart was stirred’: τοῦ is the genitive of the pronoun ‘of him’, Odysseus, and ὠρίνετο the imperfect passive of ὀρίνω ‘stir’. ἀνὰ ῥῖνας is ‘up through the nostrils’. δριμύ is ‘sharp, pungent’, and μένος ‘strength’ is here the rush of feeling that rises before tears; the literal line keeps ‘strength’ and the free English says what it is. προὔτυψε is ‘burst forth’. εἰσορόωντι is the dative participle, uncontracted, of εἰσοράω ‘look at’, agreeing with οἱ ‘to him’; φίλον πατέρ’ is ‘his dear father’.

sentences.t: κύσσε δέ μιν περιφὺς ἐπιάλμενος, ἠδὲ προσηύδα·
sentences.l: He kissed him, having clung round him, having leapt upon him, and spoke to him:
sentences.i: He sprang upon him, threw his arms around him, kissed him, and spoke to him:
sentences.n: κύσσε is the aorist ‘kissed’, and μιν ‘him’. περιφύς is the aorist participle of περιφύω, ‘having clung round’ (its object is the μιν of κύσσε), and ἐπιάλμενος the aorist participle of ἐφάλλομαι ‘leap upon’; the two actions are the first of the choices Odysseus weighed at 236, κύσσαι καὶ περιφῦναι, and now he does them. ἠδὲ προσηύδα is ‘and spoke to’. The plan of testing his father (240) is dropped.

sentences.t:
κεῖνος μέν τοι ὅδ’ αὐτὸς ἐγώ, πάτερ, ὃν σὺ μεταλλᾷς,
ἤλυθον εἰκοστῷ ἔτεϊ ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν.
sentences.l:
“That man, truly, here himself am I, father, whom you inquire after,
I have come in the twentieth year to my fatherland.
sentences.i: “I am that very man, father, whom you are asking after; I have come in the twentieth year to my fatherland.
sentences.n: κεῖνος is ἐκεῖνος ‘that man’, a predicate: ‘I am that man’. μέν τοι is ‘truly’, ὅδ’ ‘here’, and αὐτὸς ἐγώ ‘I myself’. ὃν σὺ μεταλλᾷς: ὃν is the relative ‘whom’, and μεταλλᾷς the contracted form of μεταλλάω ‘inquire after’. The second line is also found in an earlier speech of Odysseus and is rendered in the same way; ἤλυθον is the unaugmented aorist of ἔρχομαι, εἰκοστῷ ἔτεϊ ‘in the twentieth year’ a dative of time, and πατρίδα γαῖαν ‘fatherland’. The twentieth year contradicts the ‘fifth year’ of 309.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἴσχεο κλαυθμοῖο γόοιό τε δακρυόεντος.
sentences.l: But hold yourself back from weeping and from tearful lament.
sentences.i: But keep yourself from weeping and tearful lament.
sentences.n: ἴσχεο is the imperative middle of ἴσχω ‘hold back, restrain oneself’, here with the genitives κλαυθμοῖο ‘weeping’ (-οιο for -ου) and γόοιο ‘lament’ (also genitive); δακρυόεντος ‘tearful’, from δάκρυον, agrees with γόοιο.

sentences.t: ἐκ γάρ τοι ἐρέω·
sentences.l: For I will speak out to you:
sentences.i: For I will tell it out to you plainly:
sentences.n: ἐκ … ἐρέω is the same tmesis as in 265, ‘I will tell out’. γάρ gives the reason for the plea to stop weeping. The clause is cut short by the stop, and the second clause in the same line is a separate unit.

sentences.t: μάλα δὲ χρὴ σπευδέμεν ἔμπης·
sentences.l: and very much is it necessary to hasten all the same;
sentences.i: but there is great need to hurry all the same:
sentences.n: μάλα is ‘very, greatly’, χρή ‘it is necessary’, and σπευδέμεν the infinitive of σπεύδω in the epic ending -έμεν (Attic σπεύδειν). ἔμπης is ‘all the same, in any case’: hurry is needed even though there is much to tell.

sentences.t:
μνηστῆρας κατέπεφνον ἐν ἡμετέροισι δόμοισι,
λώβην τινύμενος θυμαλγέα καὶ κακὰ ἔργα.
sentences.l:
the suitors I slew in our house,
taking vengeance for heart-paining insult and evil deeds.”
sentences.i: I killed the suitors in our house, taking vengeance for the insult that pained my heart and for their evil deeds.”
sentences.n: κατέπεφνον is the first person singular of the aorist, ‘I killed’, the κατά-compound of ἔπεφνον, with reduplication. ἡμετέροισι is ‘our’, the house being his and his father’s, and δόμοισι the dative plural of δόμος ‘house’, a plural for one dwelling. τινύμενος is the participle of τίνυμαι ‘take vengeance for’, with λώβην ‘insult’ and κακὰ ἔργα ‘evil deeds’ as what is avenged; θυμαλγέα, ‘heart-paining’, agrees with λώβην. The sentence ends at a full stop; the speech that began at 321 closes here.
